notes.meaning: These lines match Psalm 96, and they turn the song outward to the whole world. Every nation is called to sing and to tell of God's salvation, meaning His rescue of His people, every single day. Matthew Henry, following an older bishop, sees here the salvation God promised through Christ, a theme we can praise daily because we gain from it daily and it never runs dry. God's people have a special duty to praise, but they are also to tell outsiders so that they too may come to worship Him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many later scholars think the writer of Chronicles built this hymn long after David by joining parts of Psalms 105, 96 and 106. They see it as a picture of the songs sung that day, not David's exact words.

notes.meaning: God is to be praised because He is great and above every so-called god. The gods of the nations are only idols, but the LORD made the heavens. Israel's God is real and made everything, while the nations have only statues. The Geneva Notes see strong faith here: even if the whole world followed idols, the singer would hold on to the living God.

Glory, honor, strength and joy surround God where He dwells. He is bright and blessed in Himself. One older sermon draws from this that God's people find lasting strength and gladness when they remember they are doing His will in all they do or bear.

The families of every nation are called to give God the honor He deserves and to come before Him with an offering. Matthew Henry says the offering was then the fruit of the ground, and now it is the praise of our lips and hearts (Hebrews 13:15). To worship 'in the splendor of His holiness' means coming in a holy way, for holiness is God's beauty. All the earth should humble itself and tremble before Him, because He rules and keeps the world steady so that it cannot be shaken loose from His plan.

Heaven and earth are invited to be glad because 'The LORD reigns!' The singer calls even things that cannot speak to rejoice with him at how great God's grace is. God's rule over all should bring both awe and joy to every people.

Sea, fields and forests are pictured shouting for joy because the LORD is coming to judge the earth. His coming will set all things right again. Creation itself bears witness to its Maker by its beauty and power. One scholar suggests this may be the first place in written Scripture to point to Christ's glorious second coming.

This is a well-loved worship line found in several psalms. We thank God because He is good, and His loving devotion, His faithful, steady love, lasts forever. His mercy reaches people in misery and is greater than their sin. Because His mercy never ends, our praise should never end either.

In the middle of praise, the people are told to pray for rescue. When we rejoice in God's kindness to us, we should remember fellow believers who are scattered or oppressed and pray for them as for ourselves. We belong to one another, so 'save us' is a fitting way to say 'save them.' Calling on God as 'God of our salvation' gives us confidence to ask Him to save.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many later scholars think this verse looks back on Israel's exile in Babylon, centuries after David. Keil & Delitzsch disagree, saying it fits prisoners taken in any war.

notes.meaning: The song ends by blessing God, who is praised from eternity to eternity. Then all the people answered 'Amen!' and praised the LORD. Their Amen showed they agreed with the praise in heart and voice. It was not a solo show but the whole people worshipping together.

Worship was not only for a big celebration now and then. It was to be every day's work, so David set up a fixed order. Asaph and his fellow Levites stayed before the ark in Jerusalem to lead daily songs of praise, with Obed-edom, Hosah and others as gatekeepers. No sacrifices were made there, yet prayer and praise rose to God like incense, an early sign of worship from the heart.

At this time the ark was in Jerusalem, but the old tabernacle of Moses and its altar were still at Gibeon. David left Zadok and the priests there to offer burnt offerings every morning and evening, just as God's Law required. These sacrifices had to continue. They pictured ahead of time Christ's work as the go-between who brings God and people together, so keeping them mattered greatly.

David also placed singers at Gibeon, led by Heman and Jeduthun, who were chosen by name. The main theme of all their songs was 'His loving devotion endures forever.' So both places of worship were filled with thanks to God.

The singers had trumpets, cymbals and other instruments set apart for God's worship, not the ones used at ordinary parties. Matthew Henry and Wesley say there is a big difference between everyday fun and holy joy, and that line should be kept. Other sons of Jeduthun served as gatekeepers.

differ.view: Some Christians believe musical instruments do not belong in Christian worship. They say Jesus and the apostles never commanded them, and Old Testament temple practice does not settle it for the church.

notes.meaning: With worship set in order, the people went home satisfied. David went home to bless his own household, meaning to pray God's blessing over them. Public worship does not replace worship at home. After our duty to God, we are bound to care for our families, pray for them and teach them to praise God.
